utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Counsel Radovic -- first of all, you can continue sitting. It is probably better for you. May I ask you to do us a favour? Since we may need to -- we had to yesterday, actually, redact quite a few names. I wonder whether you could be so kind as to refrain, when you mention a name, refrain from saying whether he or she was a witness or will be a witness so that we don't need to redact then afterwards. Otherwise, I have to show a lot of redactions. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best not to mention any names, Your Honour. By looking at the transcript yesterday, we saw that the description of the location where he met the soldiers was not quite accurate in the transcript, so we will repeat that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Zoran. I hope you rested.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will describe again for the Trial Chamber how and where you met those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My brother and I with our families went from Niko Sakic's house to the Vrebac shelter, about five, six, seven soldiers were there, that is, the ones that I saw, on that road when we went around Anto Pudza's house, so it was somewhere along the way towards Anto Pudza's house. All these houses are called Pudza's houses. I saw these five, six, seven soldiers, that is, on that road, there were about that number of soldiers. They were coming over this way. There were other soldiers coming. So there were five or six soldiers there, there were five or six soldiers coming towards the road from the lateral road, and I don't know how many more there were. In my judgement, there were about that many soldiers there. There may have been others there because they kept coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You described what types of uniforms these soldiers were wearing and what types of belts some of them had. Did you also notice any insignia or markings on their uniforms or one of their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could notice that there was some insignia there, it was some kind of a triangle, but it was dusk, and I could not notice anything else except that there was an insignia. There were some white belts, and I also saw several pistol holsters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we said that you had heard about some deaths. First you heard of the death of a friend of yours and Mirjan's, and later on, you also heard that there were some other people who were killed. Could you, on the basis of the information you had received on that morning of the 16th of April, create a picture of what actually was taking place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the way back from visiting our wives and families and looking down towards the main road, we could see some houses on fire, and based on the locations, it seemed as if these were Muslim houses. I did not see any Croat houses burning. What we saw down there, we were not sure whether there were any Croatian houses among them, but we inferred that these were Muslim houses. We could see some smoke rising in the direction where our houses were, but we could not see whether these were my house and the house of my brother and father. Later we learned that, in fact, these were not our houses which were on fire but some Muslim houses that were next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This you learned on the first day, that is, on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Ivica and Nikola Omazic brought the body of Mirjan Santic, we asked Ivica whether my and Mirjan's houses were burned down, and he said that they were not. He said that all Muslim houses around our houses were on fire. That afternoon, when we were going in the direction of Zume, you could see down near the road where I had first mentioned that there were additional houses there on fire, you could see more smoke, and as you looked towards the cemetery, in that part, which is also a Muslim part of the village, that's where the smoke was rising from as well as from the houses around us, so that's when you could gain the impression that the Muslims had been driven out of there, and there were also dead bodies around the road, but we had at that time believed that everybody had fled and I did not know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you place this in time? When did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The second time we went in the direction of Zume, it was about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, and when we were coming back -- so on the way back, that's when I learned about what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had heard shooting. In addition to shooting, did you hear any other sounds or noises?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that before we first left the depression to go towards Zume, we heard some screams somewhere ahead of us, that is, in the area behind our houses or somewhere around the Sutra warehouse, in that direction, but I cannot -- you could hear the mooing of cows, there was more shooting, and it was very confusing and ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, could you, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any moans, any cries for help?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not hear any cries for help, but I did hear some screams and moans, not one or two. I heard some women's voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you construe this scream to mean? Did it feel like this person was somehow threatened in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was a scream of fear, perhaps even of somebody being wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard this scream which you construed to be as somebody being threatened in some way, why did you not go to try to assist this person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was coming from the direction where the shooting was coming from, and the shooting continued. Even if I had started out in that direction, I don't know where I was to go, and I feared that I could lose my life or something. I didn't have enough courage to go over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you feared to go over there for fear of losing your own life or something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said something about Ivica Kupreskic and his arrival and about how it was he who informed you that it was not your houses which had been set on fire. Could you describe his coming? Where was he going? What did he say? What was the time when all this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we came back from Zume, my brother and I, that is, the first time when we were there in the morning, somewhere between 9.00 and 10.00 perhaps, as well as Mirko Sakic, near the house of Niko Sakic we met Niko Omazic, who, in my mind, was completely inebriated, he had alcohol on his breath, and he was going towards the depression and he said that Mirjan Santic had been killed. We rejoined those who were there in this depression and he then left and none of us dared to go -- he said that he and Ivica were going to try to somehow bring Mirjan over to where we were. At that time, the shooting had sort of subsided, there were very few scattered shots, and shortly thereafter, they brought Mirjan down to us on a ladder, and then the four of us picked him up and took him to Miko Sakic's house and left him in the shed there, and we only managed to ask Ivica about the houses at that time, and he said that it was not ours that were burning but someone else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the late Mirjan Santic, did you see the body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirjan was wearing a camouflage uniform. He had a white belt. He had the insignia of the military police and a light blue ribbon which was about 15 to 20 centimetres in length.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you again try to estimate the time when Mirjan Santic was brought to you or when you took Mirjan Santic to where you then deposited him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was after we had come back from Zume, I cannot say exactly, but it was somewhere before 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now describe what happened next on that day? In other words, you took Mirjan Santic's body there, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We returned to the depression, and later, Niko Sakic, who came over several times to us, he said that Mirjan was taken, I don't know, by either his father or by some relative in one of the houses near Niko Sakic's house. Sometime around noon, perhaps, some half an hour to an hour later, we heard the tanks. At that time, there was no shooting, so we again moved a little bit up towards our own houses. We were still in the forest, and at the top of that depression, the forest is a bit narrower, so you could see through all the way clear to the Sutra warehouse. I saw two tanks. They were UNPROFOR tanks. One was going towards Upper Ahmici and the other one towards our own houses, and then I lost sight of them and I couldn't see them any longer. While they were there, there was practically no shooting whatsoever. However, they may have stayed there for about an hour, I don't know if it was any longer than that, and then when they left, the shooting resumed again. Perhaps it was a bit more distance than it had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did the area where the shooting was going on change or was the shooting moving in space, so to speak, and in which direction, if it did?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that the shooting could be heard a bit farther off, and it was still coming from the direction of the cemetery and near the road, except when the UNPROFOR tanks left, the shooting was less intense than it had been that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did anything significant happen in the area in which you were moving that afternoon, something that you may have noticed and something that you believe you should tell the Court about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I still remember that Ivica Rajic sometime, perhaps around the time when the UNPROFOR tanks were still around, he was carrying some food for the children and women. We talked a little bit in more detail about how it was not our houses which were burning but rather the houses of our neighbours, Muslims, and according to him, most of those houses were on fire. He also said that he had seen there at my brother and father's house about ten soldiers, that two had brought Mirjan there and identified themselves to him as being Jokers. After our second return from Zume, from then until the nightfall, you could hear sporadic fire, as I said, less intense. We were at the top of this depression, and so if the shooting would intensify, we would slip down another 20, 30 metres, and if not, we would go all the way to the top of the depression to peek out, and this is how we stayed until the nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened just before dusk or at dusk?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It had already become dark, and when around the lower mosque near the school, you could hear intense fire, I assumed that there was some fierce fighting going on there, and it went on for about half an hour, and then a loud explosion could be heard, and after that explosion, we could see, again from the top of this depression and through the woods, that the minaret of the mosque was destroyed, that there was fire. You could see incendiary bullets. At that time, it gets dark between 7.30 and 8.00, so that must have been in that period of time when we saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After the minaret of that mosque was destroyed and after that, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We spent the night. After this shooting and after the mosque was destroyed, the shooting subsided. We spent the night behind the stables of my uncle, Ivo Kupreskic, but we were on a path where we could see the slope going above us, and we could see if somebody would be getting closer to us. We could see this in the moonlight. Whoever felt cold could go to the stables to get warmer, but we weren't very cold that night. We heard some noise somewhere behind my uncle's house, we didn't see what was going on, and during that night, when Ivica came to join us and to stand guard, he said that some soldiers from Novi Travnik had come, that they were wearing helmets and that they were allegedly supposed to take over from the soldiers in the village, I don't know, something to that effect, and we spent the entire night there between the 16th and 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were moving around, if I understood you correctly, you spent a certain period of time in the depression, then you went to see whether your family was okay, and then you went back to the depression. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you were moving thereabouts; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you carry a weapon all the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the rifle I got from Ivica was with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As you were moving about on that day, the 16th, were there any changes in the shelter by Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Niko came to tell us that those who were staying with him fled to the other shelter, the Vidovic's. Dragan Vidovic was there with us, and his family were staying in that shelter, so he thought that he should know about it. Then Dragan Samija was also supposed to know, and Mirko Vidovic, he was supposed to know that his family was also staying at Niko Vidovic's shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did they move?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He says that some bullets had hit the facade and the roof of the house, and they were frightened. They were afraid that someone might get wounded, so they tried to get away to this other shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You know where Jozo Alilovic's house is. I already asked you that yesterday. On that day, on the 16th of April, did you go to Jozo Alilovic's house at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had no need to do so. I had no reason to do so. I did not dare to go there. I could not go there. I never went close to that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This Jozo Alilovic, is he your age, your generation or, for example, your father's generation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That man is older than my father, and I can recall that perhaps he came to see my father at his house a few times, but he never came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And you personally never went to his house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, as far as I understood, you were afraid, you were afraid of the shooting; was that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Had you gone from the place where you were to Jozo Alilovic's house, would you have had to pass through the area where there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have had to go through the places where the shooting was the most intense, by my house, by the mosque, by the road, by the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that during the night you did not hear anything that would be noteworthy, except that Ivica Kupreskic said that a unit came to replace the others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as compared to the 16th, a question will be put: Why did you personally and the persons who were with you and who were carrying weapons stay at the position where you were? So could you please explain that? Why were you there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were in this depression exclusively and only for the following reason: If someone would come by, and we had received information concerning an attack by the Mujahedin or the Muslims, I don't know, but if somebody would come up there, that we protect this shelter, that we start shooting so that the women and children could escape. That was the only and exclusive reason why we were there, and from there where we were, we could see 50 to 100 metres in front of us because we would be moving back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: However, after this answer, there is an inevitable question. You saw that the army, the Croatian army, was moving in front of you. The question is wasn't this sufficient security for your families?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: How could we have known what would happen, who would attack who and who would win and where the attack would be launched? If the attack comes from Barin Gaj, and I saw five or six men and then another five or six men, 20 men or so, what could we do at any rate? But we had no idea. We knew that the women and children were there. Let us be there. Honestly, I did not expect anything to happen, as was the case before that, but unfortunately, that did not turn out to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any anything else to say concerning the 16th of April that I did not ask you about or that you did not say or have we taken care of the 16th of April altogether?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if this is important. My brother and I, when we were in the shelter, my brother with his wife and I with my wife and children, I heard rumours that someone, Milutin Katica or some other woman, because there were quite a few of them, that they called relatives or friends, whoever they have, in Mosunj, Vitez, Krizancevo Selo, et cetera, to see whether they knew what was going on over there, and they heard allegedly that there was shooting in Vitez, that in Mosunj it was peaceful, that in Poculica there was shooting, and that actually Croats had fled from Poculica too to Krizancevo Selo, and then I realised that this was really a war, that it wasn't as harmless as it might have seemed at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to the 17th, and at the end, we are going to make the necessary markings. We don't want to interrupt you now. Now tell me about the 17th. What happened on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the morning, at daybreak on the 17th, I don't remember whether this was immediately at daybreak or half an hour or an hour after that, but at any rate, in the morning, again there was shooting, but it could not be heard from down there, from the road and the cemetery, but from the middle part of Ahmici, and it was not as intense as it was the previous day. There would be shooting and then it would stop in the morning. We took turns going to see our families, to see what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As you went to see your families, did you reach a place where there was a telephone, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a telephone in Milutin Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And did the telephones work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. I already said that on the 16th, some persons called from there, made telephone calls to Vitez and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a telephone in Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was his telephone in order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th, did you personally make any phone calls to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At one point, this was in the afternoon of the 17th, perhaps it was even earlier, Niko told us that he had been to the Vidovics' shelter, the one in the middle, and that with the Croat women and children, the Bilici from Strmonje were there too and there were Muslims that were there who had fled and who were hiding with them. I think that he told Mirko that we should try to establish contact. He knew that Mirko worked at the IRC, and he thought that perhaps UNPROFOR could come and help. I'm not sure. As far as I can remember, I think he said that they also wanted to leave and that they were afraid and that there were people who were killed and that houses were being set fire to, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You did not say which Mirko you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm talking about Mirko Sakic, that is, Niko's son. Niko lived on the ground floor and he lived on the first floor of this house. So Niko and I went upstairs to his place, and he made a telephone call. I was just present. He called Ranka Gotovac, who worked in the IRC in Vitez. It is some kind of a humanitarian organisation. She spoke English, and he briefly told her what was going on and asked her whether she could try and do something. After that, I did not receive any information. We heard that some UNPROFOR tanks had come to Pican's cafe, but as far as I know, they did not come all the way to these shelters in order to take these people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these people who were staying in the shelters with the Croats, did they stay alive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I heard, yes, that they were all alive. I tried to call when I was at Milutin's house too. I tried to call Ivan Josipovic in Vitez to see whether he knew anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did Ivan Josipovic do? Why did you call him? Why did you think that you could get useful information from him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was my friend. He worked in the same company that I worked in. I did not find him. I called Zdravo Matkovic; he also worked with me. I didn't find him either. His wife answered the telephone, and she only confirmed to me what others were saying the day before that, that is to say, my wife and the others over there, that there was shooting in Vitez as well, that there was shooting on that day as well, that she heard that there were people who were dead, that some Muslims were being taken away to the cinema, and that some soldiers dressed in black were coming in. I think that she said these were the PPNs. I don't know how she knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What does PPN mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are some kind of units for special purposes. I don't -- is it the Vitezovi or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let us define this. PPN is an abbreviation for "special purpose units"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I called Majda too. When Marica, Zdravo's wife, told me that, I asked Majda also what was going on, and she told me, frightened, things that were similar to those that Marica had told me about, that she was afraid, that she saw some soldiers who were unknown to her. She would not have been afraid had she known these people. I can't remember whether she told me that they came to her door as well, they came to somebody else's door, and she heard that Muslims were being taken away and that was it. I asked whether there were any Croats nearby; perhaps they could go to that apartment to seek shelter. As far as I can remember, she also asked me about my family, where they were, and I told her very briefly that they were at Zume, that they were in shelter there, that I had fled, that there was chaos here, and that I could not understand what was going on, that it was terrible. So we just had a short conversation. That was it. I tried to phone some other people as well, but I did not manage to get through, so we returned after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did any of the people who were staying with you in these shelters, were they moving anywhere in that way, did they move in the direction of Gornja Rovna, did anybody go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, in the evening, it got dark, it was already 8.00 or 9.00, Mirko Sakic went to Niko Vidovic's shelter to see his family, and when he came back, he said to us that he did not find anyone over there. I think that he only said that he saw Pero, Pero Vidovic, an old man, perhaps 70 years old, and he said that everybody had fled to Gornja Rovna. I don't know who came to say that the Muslims attacked Krtina-Mahala, that is a place above Santici, perhaps two or three kilometres to the north, towards Poculica. My brother and I were terrified and wondered what happened to our own folks, and my wife and three children, I wondered what she could do on her own, so we went to see what was going on with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I found my wife and children at Milutin's house, and there were others that were with her there, and they told us that they had started to flee as well, but -- I am not sure whether it was Gordana Vidovic or someone else had learnt that people, civilians, elderly, women, and children from Mahala had fled and had come to the Vrebac shelter, which was by then already empty because the people who had been there had fled to Rovna, and they said that there had been an attack there, that some hay had been set on fire, but that the people who were on the front had repelled the attack, that it was halted, and my wife, Milutin's wife, and Didaci, Milka Vidovic and Gordana Vidovic came back and stayed in Milutin's house. We stayed there briefly and then went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as I understand, the 17th of April was not an eventful one for you, you were more or less mere observers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we watched, we kept guard, we kept checking with our family to see how they were, then we were inquiring to see what was happening. We could see everything on fire. All the houses more or less around the mosque and the mosque itself was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, in the area that you were moving in and from which you were observing, did you see any dead bodies on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Apart from Mirjan Santic, I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So until the end of the 17th, you had seen only that one killed Croatian soldier and you had heard about some killed Muslims, but you yourself had not seen anyone else; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, what happened on the 18th or, rather, the night between the 17th and the 18th and then proceed with the 18th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The night between the 17th and the 18th was one that we spent more or less in the same place as we had been the night before. It was possible to get some sleep in the stable because we were all very exhausted, but we didn't sleep for long. So that is how we spent the night until it dawned the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When dawn came on the 18th, was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 18th, we could hear shooting in Gornji Pirici and Gornji Ahmici. It was further away than it was on the 16th and the 17th, but we could still hear it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, the morning of the 18th, did you muster the courage to go and see what had happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the morning of the 18th, when there was a lapse in the shooting, as on any other day, we found time to visit our family and my brother went to Rovna because he hadn't seen them that night, and I remember that sometime around noon, we went to the house -- I think it was about noon, I don't know exactly -- my brother and myself and Vrebac, the two of them went to see his house and I went to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How far did you go together?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as my father's and brother's house. Then they stayed there, entered the house, and I went on to my house, which is some 20 or 30 metres away from there. I entered my house. The door was not damaged, it was intact. I entered. Nothing was wrong with it except for a broken window in the bedroom and the window facing northwards. Everything else was normal. I spent a little time there and then I went back. My brother --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute, please. The damage that you saw in your house, as no one had entered the house, would you say that it was due to some causes from the outside or from the inside?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had double-glazed windows, and the window in the bedroom was totally shattered, and the window on the north, only the outside glass was broken, not the inside glass. So the damage was caused from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about the situation around your house or on the stretch of land between your house and your brother's house; did you see any traces of any soldiers having passed by or undertaken any operations there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't stay long in my house. I reached my brother's house and waited for them to come down because they went upstairs to the first floor where he lived, Zdravko and Mica, and I was able to see an ammunition box that was empty outside the house. I also saw some casings. That is what I was able to see. And I saw Muslim houses. I think two of those houses were intact, as far as I was able to see; the others were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go inside your brother's house or did you wait for him outside, in front of the house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't go inside. I waited outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When your brother came out of the house, what did he tell you about the condition of his house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw that the door upstairs, the entrance, had been broken down, and he told me that. He also said that inside, the fridge door had been broken, he had found it in the middle of the kitchen or, rather, the dining room, and that some things had been stolen, I don't know, some jewellery and a jacket, and he and Zdravko took the accordion, and we went back to the stable. The two of them took the accordion. Zdravko came to Niko Sakic's house by car, and I stayed on next to the stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After visiting your houses, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I stayed in the stable, and the two of them took the accordion to Niko Sakic's house. They got into the car, and I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did they come back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, my brother did come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone appear who upset the rhythm of life that you had during the 16th, 17th, and part of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the afternoon, maybe at dusk, maybe it was around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, we were there next to the stable when, from the valley, several military policemen appeared, I think about four of them, and with them a group of seven or eight men in civilian clothes, some of whom I knew from Vitez. They told us that we must go with them to Gornji Pirici where a front line had been established and where trenches had to be dug and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do as they asked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had no choice. We had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: These men, these military policemen from Vitez, how were they dressed and were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, almost all of them were in civilian clothes. I think they were all in civilian clothes and that they had -- not all of them, but four or five of them had rifles. There were some without rifles too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And you set off. How did you move, in a line, in a row? How?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a line. The policemen went first, then the people from Vitez, then us. At that moment when they came, I was there, my brother, Dragan Vidovic, Mirko Sakic, Ivica Kupreskic, and I think Dragan Samija too. I don't know whether there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you were moving one by one. What position did you hold in that line of people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirko Sakic and myself were at the end of the line. He was the one but last; I was the last.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The place where you were picked up by the military policemen, how far is that place from the place where you were taken? Of course, I don't expect you to give us a precise estimate but a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It may have been 500 to 600 metres, maybe even 700, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go along a path, across the fields? What route did you take?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We passed the stable by Branko Kupreskic's house. Then we reached Enver Sehic's house, our neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As you went along from the starting position to the position where you ended up, did you see anything? If so, tell us what.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At a distance perhaps of some ten metres from Enver's house, in front of his house, I saw a body covered with a blanket or a cover of some sort. Mirko and I went up to see closer, and I recognised Enver. The house had been burnt down. I cast a glance through the window of that house, and I was horrified by what I saw inside that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I know it's not easy to tell us about these things. Do you need a rest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: He is in a rather bad state, and the memories are very terrible.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, when that picture comes to my mind, I start crying every time because that child used to play with my older son, and my wife would feed him, just like she fed my own son. The child was half burnt, and I vomited. Please, if I can have just five minutes to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Shall we take a ten-minute break? Is that sufficient for you, Mr. Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is ten minutes enough or shall we ask Their Honours to have our regular break now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Ten minutes will be sufficient. --- Break taken at 9.58 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I appreciate your gesture, and I apologise. I will try to focus better, but this just came over me, and I could not hold myself back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anything else while taking that road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that Mirko told me, he said, "Who knows what happened over there," and we could see several more bodies. One was on the balcony of a house adjoining Enver's house, which would have been about 50 metres away from us, and an additional two bodies in between those two houses in the direction of Pirici, which was also about 50 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Sakib Ahmic's house on one of those days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Looking in the direction of Pirici, the ground is rising, and when we turn around, we could see the entire village, and it was terrible. Everything was burned down. Everything was destroyed. You could feel the smoke in the air. You could see Sakib's house, but I did not approach that house at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But when you were near your house, could you see Sakib Ahmic's house from there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I could see it from there. It had burnt down, both the house and the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you approach his house at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I did not leave the vicinity of my house at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now you came to the place where the military policemen had taken you. Was anybody there at that location or were you the first ones who were brought to that location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some people were off to the left of us. There was a Muslim cemetery in Upper Pirici. You could hear somebody digging, and we were ordered to dig there where we had been brought, which was -- there was some kind of a fence, and about 20 to 30 metres up above there was Gavro Vidovic's house. I know that Mirko Sakic and I were there together on our knees and were digging a trench from that position, and to the right of us about 20 to 30 metres, there were another two men, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you dig your own trench or did somebody dig it for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we dug it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any exchange of fire at that location between you and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we arrived up there, it was still light, but about half an hour to an hour later, it had grown dark. There was some sporadic fire coming from Barin Gaj, there was a forest there, and from our side, a few bullets were fired. We did not dare get up, so this is why we were digging crouching.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Muslim soldiers at all or you just knew that they were there and that they were firing occasionally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I assume that the Muslims were up there because I could hear shots being fired occasionally from Barin Gaj, but I did not see any Muslim soldier, either on the 16th or 17th or 18th or until the end of the war personally. With my own eyes, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In this location where you were, can you say how long the military policemen who had brought you there stayed in that location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were there. When they ordered us to dig, they were lying in the grass behind us, and I recall that the people from Zume started to go home to bring something, and one of the policemen shot a burst of fire over their heads, and these men became frightened and turned around, came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many were you in that location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how many we were in that location, but those of us who were down near the barn, the ones that I have already mentioned, and the seven or eight from Vitez, those were the ones who were deployed near Gavro's house and to the right of that in groups of twos or threes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military policemen, in this location, tell you who you were going to take commands from, in other words, somebody who would be in charge, somebody who would be your commanding officer, even if it was a squad commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they did not say anything, but Slavko Papic came around that night, and on the basis of how he behaved and how he told us to dig and to take care of ourselves, I assumed that he was some kind of a commanding officer, but I did not know what kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many days did you stay in this location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were there perhaps two or three days because Slavko kept telling us how we needed to move off to the right, and we were afraid that if we moved all the way to the right, we would come to an area just above Upper Ahmici, and out of fear and uncertainty, we didn't know what was there, we didn't know whether there were any clearings, and we didn't want to go there. However, after two or three days, we were made to move over there, about 500, 600 metres to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in that location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first night when we moved over there under the cover of dark, we were all fully awake, and we were around some trees, we had some type of a cover there, and we were looking at the clearing in front of us, and then during the day, we again dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In this new sector where you found yourselves now, were there any offensive operations, either by the Muslims or by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Except for some shots fired, there was practically no fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you there in this location personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was there for about three to four months, perhaps until August, July or August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with you there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlatko Matosevic came looking for me, and by this time, I knew that he was a commander of one sector of this defence line because he had been there before, and he told me that Anto Bertovic wanted to talk to me and that I should come with him to the railroad station. I went there, and he asked me to become the commander of that sector of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was the size of the unit that you were supposed to take command over?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was a company, and Anto Bertovic was a battalion commander. I refused this. I did not want to take on that. The commander was the late Ratko Vidovic, Dragan Vidovic's brother, the Dragan whose nickname was Dragance from Zume. Anto Bertovic probably knew that I was a reserve commission officer and that I perhaps could assist in fortifying the positions and just to organise matters there. I only said that I could help the late Ratko, but I did not want to be a commander. He agreed with that, then he called Ratko and said that I would be his deputy commander. After that, we had a command post in Zume, in the house where the shelter had been, that Vinko Vidovic's shelter had been organised. I took a list of personnel from Ratko. We had a typewriter and I wanted to type up a clean list of it. We also started writing daily reports for the battalion, so I did that as well and I continued to do it until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your duties as the deputy commander consisted of keeping up the administration and writing reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What happened after I left the trenches, after three or four months, I replaced my rifle with the typewriter, so to speak, so I was mostly involved in administrative work, and those were the duties I carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it wasn't until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This is not relevant in terms of the indictment, but please describe what you did until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ratko Vidovic, the commander, was killed in September, and Ilija Azinovic replaced him, and I remained the deputy commander, and then Josip Plavcic replaced Ilija Azinovic and Ljuban Santic replaced me. However, I remained behind with a company to do the administrative work. And perhaps in January or February 1994, Bertovic transferred me to the battalion command staff, and then there was a woman who left to go somewhere else, and I did the same thing that I did in the company for the battalion, that is, I was at the typewriter typing up administrative work. Soon thereafter, the ceasefire came into effect, and so I was very involved in compiling lists and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I am now going to ask you to make certain markings on a copy of the aerial photograph. It may be better if you try to do it on the ELMO so that everybody could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please first mark the path you took on 16 April, 1993, when you were evacuating your family and, of course, you were there with your brother and his family, so please, a full line, and the end point should be Milutin Vidovic's house where your family was taken.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark with number 1 Milutin Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you encountered soldiers on your way, so please, along this path, show the location where you encountered the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now please mark on this map the position closest to your home which you reached on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now please mark the path you took on 17 April from the position where you were at the barn to the location where you joined the front line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark the final point, the point where you finally ended up, with number 5.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please mark the position of trenches on the front line and then where did you move after that first position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks) I marked the positions at the first location, and the second position is outside of what is in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If that is outside, then just leave it as it is. Thank you, Mr. Usher. On the 18th of April, you were taken to the front line. At what moment do you think you became a soldier, actually?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Practically from this 18th at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Being taken away by the military police from the positions where we were to the front line to dig trenches, can that be considered an act of mobilisation, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a kind of -- although there are no regulations to that effect, we were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, had this been mobilisation according to regulations, you would have reported there where you had your war positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that was mobilisation but not one according to regulations, but the fact was that you were taken to the front line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did you stay in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to work again sometime in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you saw the sheets that the Prosecutor showed us where it is mentioned how long you stayed in the army.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: A different date is mentioned there. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I would like the accused to be shown this document which will show exactly on which date he was demobilised. Would you please put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be D24/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on this document? It shows that your demobilisation was requested by your company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. As soon as the ceasefire was signed, I asked the battalion commander to demobilise me so that I could go back to work, but he didn't let me until I found a replacement, someone who would do what I did, so perhaps two months had gone by until I managed to -- until I managed to find a person who would do that, and then he agreed to demobilise me and then I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And then you continued to do the same thing you did before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you went back to work and when you were demobilised, where did you live then with your family? Did you stay in Ahmici, because your house remained intact, or did you go to live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not after what had happened. I did not spend a single night there. I don't know if I will ever be able to. This affected me terribly. And after the war, the refugees from Zenica came, stayed in the house, and I remained in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you already knew at that time what had happened in Ahmici. What would you say today? What is this that had happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A terrible crime had happened, and a sane mind cannot justify it or understand it. I cannot understand it. It was committed by animals. It was committed by demons. They're not men. I just don't understand how they did it all. Simply a horrible crime. It is sad that it's a crime committed by the Croat people, the people I belong to. I'm ashamed to belong to these people, but I believe that this shame will be eliminated when the culprits are found and sentenced. I live in the hope that I will live to see that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in any way in that which happened on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was thinking, my God, could I have done a single thing, a single thing in addition to what I had already done on that day? I was born there, I lived there, always in peace and friendship with all people, regardless of their ethnic or religious backgrounds. Had I had any possibility, any small chance, I certainly would have helped. Had I dreamt of what would happen, what had happened, I would have helped. However, this was a question of destiny, that I was born in Ahmici, that I had to be there. I cannot find any fault of my own. If I made any mistake in terms of what I did, I'm prepared to answer for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: During the trial, you heard all the witnesses that were heard, and you also heard that some of the Muslim witnesses have mentioned you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is your explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My assumptions can only lead to the following, that Muslims, our neighbours, heard shooting from the Kupreskic houses. That was being said time and again, "from the Kupreskic houses," "from the Kupreskic houses," and since they did not know the people who had done this, many of them had seen these people but they did not recognise them, they instinctively linked the houses and the people who lived in those houses, and that's us. They did not say our names straightaway, but as time went by, I mean, how could there be indictments if you did not have any names? So people linked this to our names and said that's us. Zoran's house is Zoran, Mirjan's house is Mirjan, et cetera. That is the only thing that I can assume, that that is how we found ourselves in these indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that you were indicted by the International Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the newspapers, I found out in 1995, and after that, the Sarajevo Vecernje Novine, I believe that's what they're called, wrote about the details of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you found out about the indictment, where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After you found out about the indictment, did you go somewhere from Vitez? Did you hide or did you remain at the very same position throughout, in the company, at home, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I worked in the company throughout, I stayed at my apartment throughout, and I always stayed in town. I never hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard about the indictment, did you try to take action vis-a-vis those people who could do something? Did you try to tell them that you were not the one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, it was unbelievable to me. I know where I was and I know what I did. How come I was indicted? And then as time went by, we saw that this was serious. First I thought it was a mistake and that someone would realise that this was a mistake and that after that, perhaps somebody would come and talk to us. However, nothing came out of that. We were prepared to talk to whoever wished to talk to us, just so that our voice could be heard too. Since we did not manage to get any further, we talked to the president of the municipality, with the president of the HDZ, with some other people in the municipality, and we said, "Well, here we are. Here we are the way we are. What can we do? We are not guilty. Can we talk to someone?" We wrote some letters to that end about our own opinions, and how much we knew, that's a different question. We wrote to the representatives of the International Community, to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that we also wrote to the Tribunal. We signed these papers, and we sought ways and means of seeing someone, talking to someone. We wanted to surrender, but how could we surrender? To who? We'd be killed. We did not succeed in achieving very much. These letters that we sent to various individuals, did they actually reach the addressees? We were told that these letters had reached the addressees, and whether they did, we don't know. We also wrote to Alija Izetbegovic, to Kresimir Zubak, and whoever was a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from among the Serb people at the time, I don't know, but we wrote to him too. We were told that these letters had reached their offices, but we never received anything by way of reply from any one of them, and in 1997, we came.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps think of surrendering to SFOR?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we heard that SFOR had killed a man when an attempt was made to arrest him in Prijedor or wherever this was, we didn't dare do that either. I felt like an animal who was destined to be shot. However, I did not hide. Many times, my child would tell me, "Daddy, there's SFOR." My child already understood from everything he heard. My wife tells me that he's traumatised until the present day. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, what is the life that your family leads nowadays?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My family lives from the aid it receives from an office. There is an office in Mostar for social aid, and I think our family gets 700 or 800 marks. I don't know exactly. They also live from the help they receive from my friends in Vitez who are involved in business. However, this comes from time to time. You do not have a permanent source of income. My mother is on her own. She has the two of us, and both of us are here. Her pension is 100 marks, and she lives in the house in Ahmici until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about your father?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My father had a weak heart anyway, even before, and at the end of September 1993, my brother and I were in the trenches at the front line above Ahmici. I was deputy commander of a company, and I was moved to a command post, and there was an attack at Barin Gaj. There were men who were killed, and he was wondering whether it was one of us, and his heart couldn't take it any longer. He died.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded. Thank you. Perhaps now we could move on to our customary break, and then my colleague, Mrs. Glumac, will continue with the questions that I did not put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thirty minutes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like to tender these last exhibits into evidence, please, the decision on demobilisation and the markings that have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection from the Prosecution. They are admitted into evidence. Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you said during your defence that Mirjan Santic was a member of the military police. Actually, you described his clothing, his uniform. My question is do you know that he was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do because I saw him at the checkpoint at the railway station, which is about halfway from my house to Vitez. I went to work by bus on a daily basis, and he was there with some others at the checkpoint, but they didn't stop the bus. We just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So he was in the traffic military police, as far as you know, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I shall now show you a document which I would like to ask you to look at, and I should like to tell Their Honours that we were given this document by the Prosecution. As far as I was able to understand, it is one of the documents that was seized during the search of the premises of the defence department in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D25/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the date? The date is the 16th of April, 1993. According to your knowledge, is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of April, 1993, in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Then the place and manner of killing, it says that Mirjan Santic was killed in Ahmici, in Vitez, during an attack of the mosque at the defence line, killed with a sniper round. According to your knowledge, is this also correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how Mirjan was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the place.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know when his body was carried, whether there were any traces of bullets or, rather, were you able to see where he was shot?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can recollect, he had some blood on his back, just below his shoulder blade. I think that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had any mask on his face, whether he had anything on his face that you could remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you said that you were the deputy commander of a company in the Vitez Brigade, are you familiar with these forms that were filled in when somebody was killed, when a soldier was killed? Are you familiar with this form?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally wrote reports about killings, but when I became deputy commander only, because until then, nobody did that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said in your testimony, for the sake of clarification, that throughout the war, from the 16th of April, 1993, you did not see a single Muslim soldier. Could you explain what you meant? How and where were you during the war? I am not thinking of the period when you were in the command but the first part of the war, when you were near Pirici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the first three days, the 16th, 17th, and 18th, I was in such a position that I couldn't see. I've already said that I couldn't even tell which house was burning, never mind identify a person. And on the 18th, at Pirici, the distance between where I was and Barin Gaj is about 200 or 300 metres and it's wooded and, again, I couldn't see anyone. But when we moved to Ahmici, the separation line was such that the Muslims were in Barin Gaj and we were lower down, and again I didn't see anyone. So that is why I said that I never personally saw a Muslim soldier on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They also had trenches in Barin Gaj, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We could hear digging over there, just as we were digging over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the distance separating the Muslim and Croat positions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depended on the place. Sometimes the distance was 50 to 60 metres and in some places it was 200 or 300 metres. Regarding where we were, in Ahmici, the distance may have been about 200 metres because there was a clearing and then a hill and a wood. They were in the wood and we were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court whether those lines shifted during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the part where we were, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During the ceasefire, was the front line the same as it was on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war, it was in the same place, and when the ceasefire was signed, people were demobilised from those front lines where we had been on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Another point that I think is unclear in the transcript, so could you please repeat it, and I am referring to the point where you reached the Sehic house on the 18th and saw that Elvir Sehic and his son were dead there -- Enver, Enver Sehic and his son.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what did Mirko Sakic say to you then? You said that you more or less had a nervous breakdown, that you cried, and what did Mirko Sakic say to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said I should keep quiet and not cry too much. He spoke to me about the military police, he said, "Can't you see them?" And probably intuitively he linked them to this because we saw something like that that morning, on the 16th, so he hurried me up to follow them uphill just in case they might come back, or I don't know what. In any case, he calmed me down so that my crying would not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Will you please look at another document now? I would like the usher to assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D26/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Have you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This document, if we can call it that conditionally, was drafted, according to the date, on the 22nd of October, 1992. In the first part of your testimony, you said that you think that it was on the 22nd, sometime around noon, that Fuad Berbic came to see you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and Muris.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that you took Fuad Berbic and Muris Ahmic to Nenad Santic's house; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you explain upon whose request you took the two of them to Nenad Santic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already recounted this, and as far as I can remember, the aunt of Ivica Kupreskic said that Nenad Santic had called and inquired about the Kupreskics, where they were, that Fuad should come by and that they should bring him over to see me. After that, Fuad called up by phone, again, the aunt, and I answered, and he said to me that he needed to go and see Nenad and was it okay for him to come? And I said, "Of course. Why not?" And he said "I'm coming." And a little later he came, together with Muris, and we went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was with you? Who went with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Myself and Miroslav Pudza with the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Fuad Berbic and Muris Ahmic had any weapons on them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, neither one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was next to Nenad Santic's house when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was Nenad, Zeljo Livancic, and Nenad's brother Vlado. I can't remember anyone else being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you in the house or next to the house; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In front of the house. There's a table outside, and that is where we sat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was discussed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I must say that I remembered that such a meeting was held, but I forgot that any paper was written, and when we were shown this paper by the Prosecution, I remembered it because, anyway, I saw my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We didn't get this paper from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I'm thinking of the other one. After that, I told my wife that she should see with Vesna, Nenad's wife, whether there was anything else, and then they found this other paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: My question was: What was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here it can be seen that I too had forgotten that Sakib was there too, but I see from the document that he was and I remember that he was. He's an elderly man, a friend of my father's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It is not the Sakib Ahmic who is your neighbour, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Will you please tell the Court what was discussed? What did Fuad say on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't recall verbatim, but I can tell you as far as I can remember what was said in summary form. I know that Fuad mentioned the fact that he had received orders from Vitez, from Sefkija, to put up a roadblock near the cemetery, but that he didn't want to do that because he felt that this could cause problems. And because he didn't want to do it, he was replaced, and Muris Ahmic was appointed in his place as commander. He carried out the order to set up a roadblock. Fuad then admitted that he didn't want to do it, and he assumed that this could cause a problem, but this young man didn't understand that, he simply followed orders; and he admitted that they were to blame for doing it, but that he had come to see if a solution could be found, the situation could calm down, and if people could go back to their homes. He hadn't left his house, but the other people from Donji Ahmici had fled on that day. That is what was discussed. I know that Nenad also blamed the Muslims for this conflict and Fuad acknowledged it. Fuad also knew that we, the local Croats, had not taken any part in it. I said that I don't remember whether we went there twice or once, but this first piece of paper was written in my handwriting. I wrote ordinary minutes, a record, on the basis of what people were saying, but I see that it was interrupted because Muris had to go up to the village to see who of the people who were manning the barricade were ready to surrender their weapons because the demand was that if they wanted to come back to the village, they had to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: From these minutes, one can also see what Sakib said, I mean Sakib Ahmic, when he says that what had happened was foolish and that Kaknjo and Sefkija needed to be called. Who was Kaknjo and what is his full name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said earlier on that he was an electrical engineer who worked in our company, and after the elections, he was president of the executive board of the municipality. The number 1 man was Ivan Santic from the HDZ and number 2 was Fuad Kaknjo from the SDA, and I remember that Sakib was embittered when he heard Fuad explaining the situation and this order that was issued. Sakib lived near the road, and close to his house, one house was set on fire on the 20th and another house of Mehmed Ahmic's, and so Sakib was very upset and indignant. I kept the minutes, and that is why I took down what he said. I thought the meeting would go on, and that is why I wanted to take notes about it, but it was interrupted, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mention is also made here of a person called Sefkija. What is his full name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dzidic. Sefkija Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what his position was in that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was in the TO headquarters in Mahala, near the fire brigade centre. He was commander or something, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to this record, Sakib said that those people need to be removed from their positions because they're causing problems and we want to live together. That is a direct quotation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I took down what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Muris Berbic said that he was going to the village and whoever wanted to come, he would bring back with them, that is, the people who would be ready to come with their weapons. What did Muris actually mean by saying this? How did you understand his meaning, because it's not very clear from these notes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After this discussion which was mostly between Nenad and Fuad, Nenad demanded that if those people wanted to come back, they had to surrender their weapons. As Fuad had been replaced the night before, he didn't want to interfere, so he told Muris, "You go up there and see. If people are ready to surrender their weapons, then we can all go back home." And Muris left. I don't remember whether we stayed on to wait or whether we also went back, but I think we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you recollect who signed this record? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it is Fuad Berbic's, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It is mentioned after that that this was going to be done by 1400 hours. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether Muris came back by 1400 hours, but Muris did come back and he came back alone. He said that people refused to give weapons. And then Fuad and Nenad agreed that a record be compiled, and that was the second record which I was taking notes for.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The first record which was drafted, was this the record which was dictated to you or did you draft it yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not dictated to me. I just took it myself. And I believe that Fuad had said, "Just take down notes of everything that we will be saying." I may have done it also on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit number 313, please? This document was not admitted, but it had been submitted by the Prosecution, actually, and if necessary, we have a sufficient number of copies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you able to review the document?
